# Visiting Artist Welcome and Safeguarding Notes

Fictional Cedar Lantern Dance Studio. Training fixture only; no real studio policy.

## Before the first visit
The welcome coordinator meets visiting artists at the front desk, explains the teaching rooms and identifies the staff host. The guest should arrive with the music already available on a device that can work offline. The desk can lend a cable, but it cannot guarantee a particular streaming service, account login or telephone signal. A teaching plan should contain an alternative quiet activity for a short audio failure.

Visiting artists must check in 25 minutes before their first scheduled teaching session. Return visits during the same confirmed residency use the normal staff sign-in process. The desk records the artist's preferred public name separately from any legal name needed for payment. Student-facing signs use the agreed public name only.

## The printed payment instruction
The artist welcome handout sets the guest-workshop reservation deposit at 20 dollars per participant. This instruction refers to the same standard guest workshops covered by the guest office handbook, which gives another amount. The welcome coordinator has not withdrawn the handout. Neither document contains an authority order resolving the disagreement, so report both figures and ask the office to reconcile them. A separate 20 dollar costume bag charge is unrelated even though the number happens to match.

## Underage participants and private coaching
For an adult-only guest workshop, the artist may teach without a host in the room after the duty lead signs the adult-session exception. The exception is specific to the dated session and cannot be copied to a youth workshop later that day. It does not remove sign-in, emergency briefing or room-closing duties. A person who turns 16 next week is still under 16 on today's register. The guest office's youth host requirement therefore remains relevant whenever the cohort includes a younger student.

A visiting artist must not arrange private follow-up coaching with a minor through the minor's personal messaging account. Requests go to the office and the guardian receives the proposal. The artist can discuss a general class exercise during a supervised session, but should not exchange a private booking link or ask a student to hide a message. A guardian's presence on site does not automatically authorize an unrecorded private appointment.

## Demonstrations and touch
Explain the purpose of a physical correction before offering it and wait for an affirmative response. A student can choose a verbal cue or a demonstration at any time. The guest should not ask the group to vote on one student's comfort. Consent for one correction does not imply consent for another or for a photograph. The host can interrupt an exercise if a student's choice is not being respected.

A student who declines touch stays in the learning activity where practicable. The visiting artist may mark the pathway in the air or show the action on their own body. Notes after class describe the accommodation factually and avoid labels about attitude or commitment. A concern is reported through the host and duty lead rather than debated in front of the group.

## Shared teaching and shortened sessions
If the named guest is replaced by another artist, a fresh booking confirmation is required even when the workshop title stays the same. The replacement supplies a new biography and receives their own host briefing. Students can then decide whether the revised event suits them under the office's cancellation offer. A guest's assistant leading a five-minute demonstration while the guest remains present is recorded as support, not as a hidden replacement.

## Sound, privacy and departure
The guest checks the music level from the edge of the room as well as from the speaker. A track containing spoken personal information should not be used for a public demonstration. After the final class, the guest returns keys to the desk, removes temporary device pairings and leaves the attendance folder with the host. Any object found in the room goes into the dated lost-property envelope rather than the artist's travel bag.

## A host handover scenario
A visiting choreographer works with adults in the morning and a mixed youth group in the afternoon. The duty lead signs the adult-session exception only for the morning. At lunch the artist reads the afternoon register and notices a 15-year-old participant, so the office arranges a host for that whole session. An enthusiastic student asks about private coaching; the artist gives the studio office address instead of requesting a personal account. The two sessions share a room and guest, but the host permission remains session-specific. Payment questions are referred with both current deposit instructions attached.

## Teaching materials and credit
If the guest supplies a short sequence to practise at home, the host records what may be shared and how the artist wants to be credited. Permission to practise a sequence does not automatically permit posting a complete lesson video. A student can keep their own plain-text reminder without being required to make a public account. Where a phrase comes from another artist, the guest can name the influence in class without implying that the other artist has endorsed the visit. Staff should ask a precise question if the sharing arrangement is unclear.

## Mixed experience groups
A guest can offer a simpler version of a task and a more complex option, then let students choose with guidance. These are teaching choices within the confirmed session rather than separate paid workshops. The host keeps the same attendance list. Do not rename a group as an advanced clinic just to avoid recording a replacement teacher. A student who rests during a difficult section remains a participant; the register should reflect presence rather than a score for effort. If the room becomes crowded, the host adjusts spacing before adding another moving group.
